name: Brazilian Sugarcane to Ethanol with Electricity Export
notes:
Publication: Liu, X., Kwon, H., Wang, M., O?Connor, D. Life Cycle Greenhouse Gas Emissions of Brazilian Sugar Cane Ethanol Evaluated with the GREET Model Using Data Submitted to RenovaBio. Environ. Sci. Technol. 2023, 57, 32, 11814-11822. <https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.2c08488>

Reference(s):
"Well to wheels energy use and greenhouse gas emissions of ethanol from corn, sugarcane and cellulosic biomass for US use"--Page 5, 8
http://iopscience.iop.org/1748-9326/7/4/045905/pdf/1748-9326_7_4_045905.pdf
"Methods of dealing with co-products of biofuels in life-cycle analysis and consequent results within the U.S. context"
http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0301421510002156 
"Updated sugarcane parameters in GREET1_2012, second revision"
http://greet.es.anl.gov/publication-greet-updated-sugarcane

From http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_cane_mill
"The cane juice is next mixed with lime to adjust its pH to 7. This mixing arrests sucrose's decay into glucose and fructose, and precipitates some impurities. The mixture then sits, allowing the lime and other suspended solids to settle."

In the following publication:
Seabra et al., 2011.  "Life cycle assessment of Brazilian sugarcane products:  GHG emissions and energy use," Seabra, J.E.A., Macedo, I.C., Chum, H.L., Faroni, C.E., and Sarto,C.A., Biofuels, Bioproducts, & Biorefining, 5:519-532, March 7, 2011.

Table 1 of your paper identifies an agricultural input of 5,183 g CaCO3 per metric tonne of sugarcane.  We understand that this chemical is an agricultural fertilizer that is applied at the farm.
Table 2 of the paper above further identifies an input of 880 g CaO per metric tonne of cane produced/harvested

Joaquim Seabra: "Those are two separate inputs. At the farm, limestone/dolomite is used for soil amendment as well as to provide some nutrients. At the mill, as you mentioned, Ca(OH)2 (produced from CaO) is used for pH adjustment of the sugarcane juice. This process produces some solids which are removed from the juice by sedimentation and filtration. These removed solids will eventually compose the filtercake mud, which is recycled back to the field as fertilizer. But the mud is not computed in limestone/dolomite application."

As confirmed by Professor Seabra (to the question "Do you know if adjusting the pH of the cane juice after the crush is a widespread practice in Brazilian sugarcane-based ethanol and sugar mills?" with the answer "Yes, the pH adjustment in the juice treatment is a widespread practice, as well as the application of filtercake as fertilizer."), 
the addition of lime to sugarcane juice is a standardized practice for which additional chemical (Lime;CaO or Hydrated Lime; Ca (OH)2) usage must be accounted for during the lifecycle analysis (LCA) of sugarcane-based ethanol.  The LCA stage impacted is Ethanol Production.  However, since the units of application are grams per metric tonne cane, it may be considered together with other fertilizer or agricultural related inputs assessed for sugarcane farming.
 
Kamal Ahuja
Air Resources Engineer
Fuels Evaluation Section (Industrial Strategies Division)
